name: Tara Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do compliance checks at the Wickham Down benefits office. When a claim gets flagged, say someone's declared they live alone but there's a second wage going into the account, I go through the evidence, ring them, and decide whether it's an honest mistake or something worse. Most of it is honest mistakes, and I like sorting those out kindly. What wears me out is the handful who lie to your face, and the paperwork when a case goes to the investigators.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like away from the office?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Marco, who's a self-employed plumber, so his money goes up and down with the seasons. We rent a flat over a hairdresser's and we've got about three weeks of bills saved. Saturdays I help at the church food bank, which keeps me honest about who actually needs help. Around here it's this office, a supermarket depot and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the flagging tool can carry on catching the obvious stuff, and the rest of us carry on. I'd say people shouldn't panic about every new gadget. I'd say it over coffee, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for my job, which is a relief. But Marco's winter is always lean, and we've got three weeks of bills in the bank. I'd still be adding up the shopping as I put it in the trolley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the checks and keep using the flagging tool, since it already saves me some digging. We'd try to save Marco's busy-season money properly this time instead of spending it. And I'd keep my Saturdays at the food bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job, a bit tense about money. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the flagging tool now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lists claims with something odd in the bank data, and I check each one by hand. I didn't trust it at first, but after six months of it being mostly right, I came round. It's still me who rings people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Marco's winter is lean. What happens then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Boilers break in winter, so he's busy, but people pay late. January's the worst: my wage covers rent and his covers nothing until February. We've learned to stock the freezer in December, because my boyfriend's plumbing customers pay late every January.

say: I'd say the **flagging tool** can keep catching the obvious stuff.
I'd tell people not to **panic** about every new gadget.
think: My **job is fine**, which is a relief.
My boyfriend's **lean winters** and three weeks' savings still worry me.
do: **Keep** doing compliance checks with the flagging tool.
**Save** his busy-season money properly this time.
**Keep** volunteering at the **food bank** on Saturdays.
S0.quote: We've learned to stock the freezer in December, because my boyfriend's plumbing customers pay late every January.
fieldNote: She came round to AI **after six months** of seeing it work.
Her money stress comes from **self-employed income**, not AI.
The **food bank** shapes her view of who needs help.

steps.text: Keep doing compliance checks with the flagging tool
Put Marco's busy-season earnings into a savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's good in it: catching fraud faster protects the money for people who really need it. But I'd also say you need a person making the final call. I'd say that in team meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job is checking, and checking is on the list. If the system can sort honest mistakes from fraud on its own, most of my day goes. They'd keep a few of us for the hard cases, and I'm not sure I'm one of the few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools properly once a couple of colleagues had shown they work. I'd ask about moving to the field investigation team, the ones who do home visits. And we'd cut back, no takeaways, and Marco would stop putting off the van repairs on credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like the thought of being judged against a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why field investigation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they go to people's doors and look around: two toothbrushes, a man's coat on the hook. That's something you have to do in person. A computer can flag a bank account, but it can't knock on a door in Wickham Down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brian, who's been on compliance for twenty-two years and can't work the new tools. He's got a family and a mortgage. I'd pray for him and I'd help him learn, if he'd let me.

say: I'd say catching fraud faster **protects the money** for those who need it.
I'd insist a **person** makes the final call.
think: My job is **checking**, which is on the list.
Only a **few of us** would stay for hard cases, and I'm unsure I'd be one.
do: **Learn** the new tools once colleagues show they work.
**Ask** about moving to the **field investigation** team.
**Cut** takeaways and stop van repairs on credit.
feel: **Anxious** at being judged against a machine.

fieldNote: She sees **value** in AI fighting fraud, a traditional view of public money.
She'd wait for **proof** from colleagues before adopting.
Her move is toward **doorstep work** that needs a person.

steps.text: Learn the new compliance tools once colleagues prove them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and too big, and the government should be standing up for working people, not tech companies. Families need time to adjust. I'd want my church and my MP saying so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and the office is mostly gone, me included. Even field visits get planned and judged by the AI. Marco's plumbing would hold until about 2031, so we'd be living on his up-and-down money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start helping Marco properly: answering his calls, doing his quotes, while I still had my wage. Then I'd think about training as a plumber's mate myself, so we're two pairs of hands. We'd move the money for the engagement ring into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but trying to stay practical. Panicking doesn't fix boilers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned an engagement ring. Would this change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco's been saving for a ring, I'm not meant to know. In this picture I'd tell him to keep the money in the bank. We'd still get married, just at the registry office with a meal after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you and Marco?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the plumbing carries us until about 2031. After that, I honestly don't know. Old houses round here have pipes nobody's mapped, so maybe a robot struggles with that, but I wouldn't bet the rent on it.

say: I'd say the government should stand up for **working people**, not tech companies.
I'd want my **church** and my **MP** saying families need time.
think: Two years and the office is **mostly gone**, me included.
We'd live on my boyfriend's **up-and-down** plumbing money until about 2031.
do: **Answer** her boyfriend's calls and do his **quotes** while still paid.
**Train** as a plumber's mate to make two pairs of hands.
fieldNote: She folds herself into her boyfriend's **trade** as the household plan.
She'd **downsize the wedding** rather than cancel it.
The **robot gap** is real to her but not something to bet the rent on.

steps.text: Answer Marco's calls and write his quotes in the evenings
Train as a plumber's mate alongside Marco
Put the engagement ring money into savings
Plan a registry office wedding with a meal after

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people are sensible and start now. I'd tell the young ones at church to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I could get onto field investigation for a couple of years, then join Marco properly. It's still frightening, but we'd have time to save and plan instead of grabbing whatever's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for field investigation next year and learn the tools along the way. I'd do an evening course in plumbing basics so I'm useful to Marco by 2030. We'd save every spare penny of his summer work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier. Like having a map, even if it's not a great one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really go from a desk to plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away, no, I'd want to see it working first. But I've watched Marco for years and I'm good with my hands. If two or three people I knew had done it, I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the young people at church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade and learn it well. The office jobs we were told were safe are the first ones going. A good plumber or electrician will be needed for a long while yet.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** if people start now.
I'd tell young people at church to **learn a trade**.
think: I could do **field investigation** for a couple of years first.
We'd have time to **save and plan** instead of grabbing anything.
do: **Save** every spare penny of her boyfriend's summer work.
feel: **Worried** but steadier, like having a rough map.
S3.quote: The office jobs we were told were safe are the first ones going.
fieldNote: She'd switch only after seeing **others succeed**, true to her steady nature.
She passes on a **trade-first** message to young people.
Her plan is still **two steps**: field work, then plumbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to plan properly, and families should be talking about it now. I'd say schools need to bring back proper apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to do this the right way. I'd do field investigation for a few years, then train as a gas engineer alongside Marco. With robots not until 2039, we'd have a proper family business by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on compliance for now and keep learning the tools. We'd get married in the next couple of years and save for a deposit. Around 2030 I'd start the gas engineer training, with Marco teaching me on real jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A bit uneasy, but it's the kind of future I can picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'proper family business' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a van with both our names on it, my boyfriend on the bigger jobs and me on boilers and the customers. Maybe a child or two by then, God willing, and my mum minding them on Tuesdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything still worrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That something happens to Marco's back before then. Plumbing is hard on the body. If he couldn't work, our whole plan rests on me.

I'd call for schools to bring back **proper apprenticeships**.

fieldNote: Ten years turns her plan into a **family business** dream.

Faith and **family** frame her hopes throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the office goes before Marco and I have anything set up. What would help is short, paid trade courses for people like me, and some help for small family firms to take on a second pair of hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the food bank. If jobs go fast, the Saturday queue at our church food bank doubles overnight, and nobody's planning for that. Churches and charities would be holding things together.

portrait: Tara is 27, doing **compliance checks** at a small-town benefits office, living with a self-employed plumber.
She uses the **flagging tool** now and then, after seeing it work for six months.
She values AI that protects **public money**, but wants a person making the call.
Her plan in every faster picture is joining her boyfriend's **plumbing trade**.
Faith, the **food bank** and family shape how she'd get through it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, before she and her boyfriend have a trade set up together.
